newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Stronger growth seen aiding EU expansion costs.
newsitem.headline: Stronger growth seen aiding EU expansion costs.

text.p: Stronger economic growth should allow the European Union to meet the costs of eastern expansion and maintain funding for some of its poorer regions and countries, the European Commission said on Wednesday.

Unveiling its plans to start accession talks with Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic, Estonia and Slovenia, also known as Agenda 2000, the EU said its current spending ceiling of 1.27 percent of Gross National Product would be maintained through 2006.
"We are looking at annual average growth of 2.5 percent (for the EU) which I think is fair in the current circumstances," Commission President Jacques Santer told a news conference.
The expected growth, which for eastern Europe was put between four and five percent, should generate an added 20,000 million Ecus ($22,000 million) by 2006.
The additional funds are expected to allow Europe's poor regions, mainly in Spain, Portugal, Greece and Ireland, to be eligible for aid between 1999 and 2006.
Total EU structural and so-called cohesion fund spending would be set at 275 billion Ecus between 1999-2005. Structural funding covers regional, social and agricultural development projects.

For the potential new members, there would be a further 45 billion Ecus of regional, social and agricultural assistance, the vast part of it -- 38 billion Ecus -- becoming available once they joined the EU.
"The priority policy goal of economic and social cohesion must be steadfastly adhered to," the Commission said.
"Indeed, the prospect of enlargement encompassing new countries with widely diverging levels of development makes this even more necessary than before."

For assistance coming under the heading of cohesion funds, there was agreement that countries whose GNP is less than 90 percent of the EU average would still benefit even if they qualify for the planned single currency.
Some powerful factions within the Commission had tried to exclude Spain, Ireland and Portugal from the fund because they are likely to meet criteria for joining the new currency, the euro, in 1999.

It was argued that if those countries were strong enough financially to meet the tough single currency membership conditions, they did not need special EU aid totalling three billion ecus annually from the fund.
The aid is used to help fund trans-European road, rail and other transport networks as well as environmental projects.
But Spain and the other three countries warned they would block any attempt to cut off the aid, saying that the terms for economic and monetary union and the cohesion fund were separate issues.
Regional Affairs Commissioner Monika Wulf-Mathies told a news conference that aid to the three countries would be judged on a case-by-case basis as economic figures became available.
